title: Solo length: a chorus is a story
summary: In early bands solos were usually one chorus; he thinks a chorus is a story of his imagination and likes two choruses on short pieces and ballads.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Like you were just talking about that stop time thing and 'How Come You're Doing Me Like You're Doing' -- the kind of solos you play in a band in those days would usually not be very stretched out, would they? (inaudible)
You mean like they played five or six chords at a time?
Well no. We played one chorus pieces. They never played -- no, the guys never played a whole lot of choruses, unless they felt like it -- unless the guys felt that they should play another chorus.

You know, you don't just force it on people -- I mean -- for me, if I don't tell the story in one chorus, then I ain't going to tell no story. You know, and I think a chorus is a story of your own imagination. So my imagination probably runs out after a chorus or so. You know.
Sometimes I like to play two choruses. Sometimes it is the length of the piece. The piece is 16 measures, I don't mind playing two choruses, you know.
Oh maybe sometimes I play a two 30 -- two choruses of 32 measures, but --
Or if it's a ballad and let's you come back --
If it's a ballad, yes, I like the ballads. I particularly like ballads better than other things. Cause I like to try and do something with a ballad.
